title: Leaders Who Attention Bomb
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article names and dissects a subtle manipulative pattern: leaders who shower a chosen team member with an intense, temporary burst of attention, favor, and access designed to build loyalty and dependence. It frames the behavior as often unconscious, rooted in the leader's own insecurity and need for control, and typically short-lived before the leader moves on to a new target. The piece emphasizes that the pattern is highly visible to the wider team, who come to distrust the sincerity of any praise or attention because they've watched the cycle repeat with previous 'favorites.' It closes with a practical corrective: leaders should notice the habit and deliberately cap and distribute attention more evenly across the team.
points: Attention bombing is described as a largely unconscious tactic used by insecure, control-seeking leaders to create loyalty and dependence in a chosen team member.
The pattern is cyclical: leaders typically move to a new 'target' every few weeks, and the team notices the rotation.
Because the team can predict who's next, it undermines trust in the sincerity of the leader's praise for anyone.
Setting explicit limits on how much attention any one person receives, and distributing praise more evenly, is offered as the fix.
quotes: Attention makes people feel special, while profuse attention makes people feel obligated.
This manipulative tactic is often unconscious and deployed by leaders who are deeply insecure and crave control.
For those leaders addicted to attention bombing, they move from target to target like a child moves from one shiny new toy to another.
The predictable attention on someone new undermines the trust and confidence the team has in the leader.
Leaders who want to break the habit must first become aware of the signs and then refrain from focusing too much attention on any one team member, no matter how worthy they might seem.
